title: Rosh Hashanah: the three sounds
hookLine: tekiah, shevarim, teruah: one long blast, broken sighs, short sobs

cards: Stand in a synagogue on Rosh Hashanah and listen. A man lifts a curved horn to his lips. A caller beside him reads out a word, and he blows one long, steady note.
Another word, and the horn makes three broken, wavering notes, like someone catching their breath. A third word, and a rapid string of short bursts, almost a stammer. Then one long note again.
Three kinds of sound, over and over, and by a custom many keep, a hundred blasts by the end of the day.

teach.b: The three sounds are tekiah, the long blast; shevarim, the broken notes, from a word meaning breaks; and teruah, the rapid short ones.

teach.h: A DAY OF TERUAH, NEVER DESCRIBED.
teach.b: The Torah calls Rosh Hashanah a day of teruah, but it never describes what a teruah sounds like. So the Talmud, in Rosh Hashanah 33b and 34a, investigates.

It notices that the old Aramaic translation renders teruah with a word for crying, and it finds the same root in the Song of Deborah, where Sisera's mother waits at her window for a son who will never come home, and cries.
So a teruah is a cry. But what kind? Maybe a groan: long, heavy sighs.
Maybe a wail: short, gasping sobs. Maybe both, sighs and then sobs, the way people really cry. Nobody could be sure which the Torah meant.

So the sage Rabbi Abbahu, in Caesarea, set an order that covered every possibility: the sighs alone, the sobs alone, and the sighs followed by the sobs, each with a long, steady tekiah before and after.
That's why the pattern is so long and adds up to so many blasts: the tradition wasn't certain, so it chose to do every version. Notice the frame, too.

The broken sounds always sit inside the whole ones: crying, held on both sides by something steady. Many teachers read it as a picture of the year. The brokenness is real, and it is not the whole story.

how: On Rosh Hashanah (except on Shabbat) the shofar is sounded in the synagogue in sets of tekiah, shevarim and teruah, a caller announcing each note; many communities reach one hundred blasts over the service.

o: the shofar's broken cry of short, rapid notes
a festive trumpet fanfare for a new king
the single long blast that ends a shofar set

games.q: inside the three sounds — tap the pairs.
p: set an order covering every version

s: the Torah explains exactly what a teruah sounds like
it never does; the Talmud has to investigate.
the Talmud links teruah to the crying of Sisera's mother
the same root appears in the Song of Deborah.
the broken sounds are always framed by long, whole ones
a tekiah before and after each set.

games.q: you're a sage. nobody knows if the Torah's teruah means sighs, sobs, or both. what do you rule?
o: blow every version: sighs, sobs, and both together.
skip the teruah until it's certain.
games.why: Rabbi Abbahu's order covers all three, which is why the blasts add up to so many.

practice: Breathe the pattern slowly: one long, steady breath out like a tekiah, three breaths out in pieces like sighs, a few quick short ones like sobs, then one long, whole breath again.
If something from this year needs a sigh, let it have one, and if you pray, let the breaths carry it to God. The long breath at the end is there to hold the rest.

wordCard.voice: Teruah. The broken cry of the shofar, whose exact sound the Torah never describes, so the tradition plays every version.

orig.note: Hebrew: the shofar's broken cry; the Torah calls Rosh Hashanah a day of teruah.

carryVoice: Your line: a sigh and a sob. With a long, steady note on either side. Day six hundred forty-six.
